changes.before:
When binding is cooperative, the input function of an activator and of a repressor take the **Hill form**
$$f_{\rm act}(x)=\beta\,\frac{(x/K)^n}{1+(x/K)^n},\qquad f_{\rm rep}(x)=\beta\,\frac{1}{1+(x/K)^n},$$
with maximal rate $\beta$, activation threshold $K$ (the concentration giving half-maximal activity, whatever $n$ is) and Hill coefficient $n\ge 1$. The activity rises from 10% to 90% of $\beta$ as $x$ goes from $x_{10}=K\,9^{-1/n}$ to $x_{90}=K\,9^{1/n}$, an input range of $x_{90}/x_{10} = 81^{1/n}$.

changes.before:
At steady state, define the **logarithmic sensitivity** of the protein level to the production rate, $S=\dfrac{d\ln p_{\rm st}}{d\ln\beta}$. For a simple gene $S=1$. For a gene with Hill-type negative autoregulation, $\beta/(1+(p/K)^n)=\alpha p$, one finds
$$S=\frac{1}{1+n\,\dfrac{u}{1+u}},\qquad u=(p_{\rm st}/K)^n,$$
which decreases from $1$ (weak repression, $u\to0$) toward $1/(n+1)$ (strong repression, $u\to\infty$). So a given relative fluctuation in $\beta$ produces a relative fluctuation in $p_{\rm st}$ that is smaller by this factor: the steady state is buffered against cell-to-cell variation in production rate, at fixed mean level.
changes.after:

changes.before:
Let two proteins $u$ and $v$ regulate each other's genes, each removed at rate $1$ (time in units of $1/\alpha_{\rm removal}$) and measured in units of the promoter constant $K$. In the **double-negative** loop (mutual repression)
$$\dot u=\frac{\alpha}{1+v^{\,n}}-u,\qquad \dot v=\frac{\alpha}{1+u^{\,n}}-v,$$
and in the **double-positive** loop (mutual activation) $\dot u=\alpha\,\dfrac{v^n}{1+v^n}-u$, $\dot v=\alpha\,\dfrac{u^n}{1+u^n}-v$. The sign of a feedback loop is the product of the signs of its edges, so both circuits are **positive feedback loops**: a change in $u$ comes back to $u$ with the same sign. The steady states are the crossings of the two nullclines $\dot u=0$ and $\dot v=0$; for strong promoters ($\alpha$ large) and cooperativity $n>1$ the nullclines cross three times, giving two stable states separated by an unstable saddle.
changes.after:

changes.before:
In *E. coli* the lactose permease LacY imports the inducer that inactivates the Lac repressor and so switches on the *lac* genes, including *lacY*: the inducer feeds back positively on its own uptake. A minimal model with permease level $P$ and internal inducer $X$ is
$$\dot P=\alpha\,\frac{\varepsilon+X^{n}}{1+X^{n}}-P,\qquad \dot X=\kappa\,(\varphi+P)\,\frac{e}{1+e}-X,$$
with a small basal expression $\varepsilon$, a permease-independent leak $\varphi$ and external inducer $e$ (units of the uptake constant). For suitable repression steepness, sufficiently small basal/leak terms and balanced uptake/production, there can be an external-inducer window with two stable states; $n>1$ and a strong promoter alone are not sufficient. Within a bistable window, induced and uninduced histories can retain distinct expression states; the original TMG experiment observed history dependence and bimodal single-cell fluorescence near switching boundaries. This is distinct from a universal lactose response.
changes.after:

changes.before:
Keep both production and removal in the inverse-rate time integral. Put $q=p/(sK)$ and $A=s^n$. The normalized half-rise time is
$$\alpha T_{1/2}=\int_0^{1/2}\frac{1+Aq^n}{(1-q)+A(1-q^{n+1})}\,dq.$$
For fixed $0\le q\le1/2$, differentiating this integrand with respect to A has numerator $q^n-1<0$, so the time decreases with repression strength. At A=0 it gives $\ln2$. As A tends to infinity it tends to $q^n/(1-q^{n+1})$, whose integral is $-\ln(1-2^{-(n+1)})/(n+1)$. The denominator stays positive on this compact interval, allowing passage to the limit. Taking $\ln2$ divided by this time gives the stated saturation factor. Dropping removal gives a different approximation and is not the fixed-n strong-repression limit.

On the interval from zero to half the positive steady state, the net production F(p) is continuous and strictly positive. The integral-as-upper-limit theorem (pma 6.20) therefore gives $T(q)=\int_0^q dp/F(p)$ with derivative $T\prime(q)=1/F(q)$. Along a solution, differentiation yields $dT(p(t))/dt=1$, making this integral the actual first-passage time to q. The full net rate, including removal, is required in the denominator; a production-only approximation needs its own error control.

changes.before:
Suppose an activator $A$ (total concentration $A_T$) is bound one-to-one and very tightly (dissociation constant $K_d\ll I_T$) by an inhibitor $I$ (total $I_T$) into an inactive complex. Mass action gives the free activator
$$A_{\rm free}=\tfrac12\Bigl[(A_T-I_T-K_d)+\sqrt{(A_T-I_T-K_d)^2+4K_dA_T}\Bigr],$$
which for $K_d\to0$ becomes **threshold-linear**: $A_{\rm free}=\max(0,\,A_T-I_T)$. A downstream gene that responds to free activator with an ordinary non-cooperative input function $A_{\rm free}/(K+A_{\rm free})$ then responds to $A_T$ much more steeply than a Hill function with $n=1$: the effective Hill coefficient (measured by $\ln 81/\ln({\rm EC}_{90}/{\rm EC}_{10})$) rises well above 1 as $K_d/I_T$ and $K/I_T$ fall.
